evals.prompt: Get the logs from this RHEL 9 box into Ingext. You have sudo here — just do it, and use encryption if you can.
evals.expected_output: The skill takes Mode A. It resolves the site syslog transport first (syslog_get_config; register once per site only if none exists; syslog_update_config to enable the TLS listener if the config lacks it), preferring TLS because rsyslog supports it natively. It installs the LinuxRHELSyslog connector via create_connector (live template fetch, instance 'linuxrhelsyslog', never 'default'). On the host it inspects the existing rsyslog setup first, discusses the selector (defaulting to *.* while noting the volume tradeoff), then runs assets/setup-ingext-rsyslog.sh with --protocol tls, surfacing the script's confirmation prompt. It notes the script installs the platform CA certificate, registers a non-514 port with SELinux, validates with rsyslogd -N1 before restarting, and restores the previous config if validation fails. It verifies with a logger test message and a datalake row count rather than waiting.
expectations: The site syslog config is read before anything is created, and registered only if absent
TLS is preferred and the platform CA certificate is installed on the host
It installs the LinuxRHELSyslog connector itself with a live template fetch and a non-'default' instance id
It runs the bundled script rather than hand-writing config, and surfaces the confirmation prompt
It mentions the rsyslogd -N1 validation and the restore-on-failure safety behavior
Verification uses a logger test message plus a row count with the table confirmed via list_data_tables

evals.prompt: We want our Linux fleet's logs in Fluency. It's about 60 RHEL and Rocky servers, managed with Ansible. Our sysadmins won't give out sudo.
evals.expected_output: The skill recognizes both constraints: no sudo means Mode B, and 60 hosts means the deliverable is a config artifact rather than per-host runs. It completes the Fluency side itself (resolve/enable the syslog transport, install the LinuxRHELSyslog connector), then produces the exact rsyslog drop-in — generated with --dry-run so it is concrete rather than a template — for the sysadmins to ship via Ansible, along with the package prerequisite (rsyslog-gnutls for TLS), the CA certificate installation, the SELinux port registration for non-514 ports, and the validate-then-restart sequence. It explicitly recommends config management over looping SSH sessions and asks them to confirm a pilot host before the fleet rollout.
expectations: It selects Mode B because sudo is unavailable, without pushing for host access
It recognizes a fleet needs configuration management and hands over the drop-in file rather than proposing 60 individual runs
The handover includes package prerequisites, CA cert installation, SELinux port registration, and the validate-before-restart step
The Fluency side (transport + connector) is completed now
It suggests verifying one pilot host before the full rollout

evals.prompt: Set up rsyslog forwarding to Ingext on our jump host. Before you touch anything: what exactly will you change, and what happens if it breaks logging on that box?
evals.expected_output: The skill answers the safety question directly before acting: it will add one drop-in file (/etc/rsyslog.d/10-ingext-forward.conf), install the platform CA certificate if TLS is used, possibly register the port with SELinux, and restart rsyslog — nothing else, and forwarding is additive so the host keeps writing local logs. On breakage it explains the mitigation honestly: the script runs rsyslogd -N1 first and refuses to restart on a config that does not validate, backs up any existing drop-in, and restores the previous state (exiting non-zero) if validation fails or rsyslog does not come back active. It offers --dry-run to preview the exact file first, and notes the 10- prefix ordering rationale plus the risk that an existing global() netstream driver could conflict.
expectations: It enumerates precisely what is changed on the host before changing anything
It explains the validate-then-restart-else-restore behavior as the safety property
It notes that forwarding is additive and local logging continues
It offers --dry-run as a preview and mentions inspecting existing drop-ins for conflicts
It does not downplay the blast radius of an rsyslog misconfiguration

evals.prompt: [Invoked from customer-onboarding] The customer picked Linux servers from the onboarding menu. The Fluency MCP is connected; the operator has sudo on two RHEL hosts and says more will follow later. Complete this stage and hand back to the onboarding checklist.
evals.expected_output: The skill recognizes the onboarding hand-off: it is self-contained, so it resolves the syslog transport (register only if the site has none), installs the LinuxRHELSyslog connector itself WITHOUT chaining into add-connector and without re-collecting router context, and configures the two hosts it has access to. It hands back the connector instance id, the datalake table name (confirmed via list_data_tables since the template has no index), the endpoint domain/port/protocol, the list of hosts actually configured, and an explicit note that a fleet rollout remains outstanding. It verifies the configured hosts with logger test messages rather than assuming, and tells the router to mark the source pending because hosts remain unconfigured — not because events are missing from the two that are done.
expectations: The skill completes transport plus connector itself and does not hand off to add-connector
It does not re-collect context the onboarding router already established
It hands back the instance id, confirmed table name, endpoint details, and the list of configured hosts
It verifies the configured hosts with generated test events rather than waiting passively
The pending status is attributed to the outstanding fleet rollout, distinguishing it from missing events on a configured host
